newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian bank AnHyp still looking for buyer.
newsitem.headline: Belgian bank AnHyp still looking for buyer.

text.p: Troubled Antwerp-based mortgage and savings bank AnHyp repeated in its annual report to shareholders that it was still looking for a partner or buyer for its retail banking operations.

"To avoid any misunderstanding, the board reaffirms its belief that for shareholders, staff and agents, it would be better to find a partner or buyer of its retail banking operations," the bank's board wrote. "This is a significant and delicate undertaking. Decisions cannot be taken lightly and several factors must be considered," it said.
AnHyp holds its annual shareholders meeting on Monday.
AnHyp, which has been plagued by bad property loans, a dispute with Belgium's tax authorities and other difficulties in the past two years, began its search for a partner bank in April 1995.
Since last August however, when it broke with advisor U.S. merchant bank Goldman Sachs and appointed Belgium's Petercam in its place, there has been little news on how the search was going.
In the annual report, AnHyp noted its property and tax problems have prevented any candidates from making offers likely to be accepted by the board.

"This is where the idea of selling only the banking activity strictly speaking came," it added, not giving details. "With the aid of a merchant bank which is well in tune with the complex Belgian realities, this idea has been explored in priority since the autumn," it added.

The board said while the search went on it was concentrating on cleaning up its balance sheet and restructuring the bank's operations. It said it was cutting back on the weight of bond and property assets in its balance sheet, while increasing other types of financial assets.

AnHyp's total assets were reduced to 292.5 billion francs at the end of 1996 from 302.5 billion in 1995. Operating profit fell to 2.85 billion francs from 3.45 billion francs, but losses narrowed to 430 million francs from 1.25 billion francs as provisions and write downs on its loan portfolio were reduced.
The board said the main shadow over the bank remained its exposure to the commercial office property market and the absence of any recovery in this sector.
It said it expected the Brussels property market to stabilise in 1997 before rents began to rise again in 1998.
